summary: Describes how to carry the Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) over HTTP. This is the transport document that RFC 4210 referred to, and it updates that reference. It is a standards-track specification. It was replaced by RFC 9811.

eli5.summary: A certificate office has its own forms and needs a way to send them. This memo says how to mail those forms using the ordinary web delivery service.

subtitle: How to carry certificate management messages over plain HTTP POST requests.

tldr.problem: The Certificate Management Protocol (CMP) needs a well-defined way to move its PKIMessage sequences between end entities, registration authorities and certification authorities.
tldr.mechanism: Each DER-encoded PKIMessage is sent as the body of an HTTP POST with media type application/pkixcmp, and the CMP response comes back in the body of a 200 response.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6712 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9811 and updated by RFC 9480.

today: RFC 6712 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 9811 and updated by RFC 9480. It updated the CMPtrans reference in RFC 4210.

sections.title: Why CMP Needs a Transfer Mechanism
sections.content:
The Certificate Management Protocol (RFC 4210) requires a transfer mechanism so that End Entities (EEs), Registration Authorities (RAs) and Certification Authorities (CAs) can pass PKIMessage sequences to each other. The first CMP specification (RFC 2510) described a simple transfer layer over TCP with error handling and polling. Since RFC 4210 has its own polling, only connection handling and error handling remain as needs.

RFC 6712 is the "CMPtrans" document referenced in RFC 4210, so it updates that reference. It describes HTTP as the only transfer protocol, because implementers preferred plain HTTP to the earlier TCP-based approach.

The RFC admits that tunneling CMP through POST is generally considered bad practice, but gives reasons: HTTP is easy to implement, it traverses network borders using ubiquitous proxies, and it is already common in CMP implementations. GET is not used because PKI operations can only be triggered by PKI messages, which need a POST.
sections.eli5: Certificate offices needed a way to send their forms. Most people already knew how to use the web, so they chose to send the forms over it.

sections.title: How a CMP Message Rides on HTTP
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support HTTP/1.0 (RFC 1945) and SHOULD support HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2616). A DER-encoded PKIMessage is sent as the entity-body of an HTTP POST, and the Content-Type header MUST be application/pkixcmp.

On success the server returns the CMP response in the body of the HTTP response. The status code MUST be 200; other 2xx codes MUST NOT be used for this purpose. Other 4xx and 5xx codes MAY be used to report errors. 3xx redirects MAY be supported, but clients should only follow them automatically after careful thought about the security implications.

The Request-URI follows RFC 3986, and a server MUST treat paths with and without a trailing slash as identical. For example, a request to the /cmp path of host example.com starts with POST /cmp HTTP/1.1.

Persistent connections are only a performance optimization. Because intermediaries can mix clients on one upstream connection, implementations MUST NOT infer that requests on the same connection come from the same client. Each message is evaluated in isolation.
sections.eli5: Put the certificate form in the envelope, write what kind of form it is on the outside, and post it. The answer must come back marked with a plain thumbs-up code.

sections.title: Workflow and Pushed Announcements
sections.content:
Most CMP communication is started by an EE, and each request triggers a CMP response from the CA or RA. If the HTTP request is not confirmed by an HTTP response, the message MUST be assumed not delivered.

Announcements are the exception. A CA may create them on events or on a regular basis and may push them over HTTP, acting as an HTTP client. The announcements are the CA Key Update, Certificate, Revocation and CRL Announcements. They are sent as a POST body, and the recipient does not send a CMP response. It MUST acknowledge with an HTTP response with an empty body.

The recipient answers 201 Created if the information was stored or was already present, or MAY answer 202 Accepted if it was only accepted for processing. The sender may then retry after a delay. A receiver MUST answer with a suitable 4xx or 5xx code on problems. An EE that wants to poll for a CA key update or the current CRL can use a PKI Information Request with a General Message.

Implementations SHOULD keep HTTP usage as simple as possible. For example, chunked Transfer-Encoding has no benefit, and clients need not use Expect: 100-continue.
sections.eli5: Usually you ask and the office answers. Sometimes the office sends out news on its own. Then the receiver just says got it, or sorry, there was a problem.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists several risks. Many open connections can exhaust a server, so idle connections should be closed after a timeout, and a server should close the connection after sending a CMP Error Message. Without a security protocol such as TLS, HTTP has no integrity protection, so information from HTTP should not be used to change the state of a transaction.

A client that stores the target of a 301 Moved Permanently response could be blocked from the correct server by a man-in-the-middle. Responses to pushed announcements cannot be trusted without protection, so a PKI design must not depend on announcements being reliably received.

CMP has its own integrity protection and authentication, and its unencrypted content is not sensitive to the PKI, but an eavesdropper might still gather confidential information. Users might want HTTP over TLS (RFC 2818) or IPsec. Compliant implementations MUST support TLS with the option to authenticate both server and client.
sections.eli5: A plain envelope can be swapped or read. So the rule is to be careful what you trust from the envelope, and to use a locked box (TLS) when it matters.
